Chapter 2: The Trauma of Violence and the Struggle to Survive.
When violence shatters a life, it doesn’t just leave marks on the body. It seeps deep, changing how someone looks at the world—and how they see themselves.
For anyone who’s survived such an attack, those first hours and days are a blur. Fear, confusion, disbelief—they all swirl together. The mind goes over every detail, trying to make sense of what happened, desperate to find some kind of meaning or control.
After a kidnapping or assault, life instantly feels foreign, and yet, painfully real. Suddenly, there are medical exams, police interviews, and strangers asking for details that feel almost impossible to share. Each question can sting like a fresh wound, forcing the survivor to relive their nightmare again and again.
Sleep? That becomes a rare luxury. Nightmares play back the violence on a never-ending loop. Even small sounds—a creaky door, footsteps in the hallway—can trigger a wave of panic. The body remembers, even when the mind wants to forget. Everyday things become overwhelming, and a constant sense of alertness sets in, never quite letting go.
Family members, desperate to help, often feel completely lost. They want so badly to offer comfort, but words just don’t seem enough. Some hover, afraid to leave the survivor alone, while others quietly retreat, struggling with their own helplessness. Suddenly, home doesn’t feel safe—it feels like a battlefield.
Healing isn’t a straight line. There are little victories—like getting out of bed or taking a short walk—and there are setbacks, days when hope feels out of reach. Therapy becomes a lifeline, a place to start untangling the guilt, shame, and anger that trauma leaves behind. Here, the therapist listens without judgment, helping the survivor slowly piece things back together.
Out in the community, responses are all over the map. Some people gather around, offering support and kindness. Others keep their distance, unsure what to say or do. Whispers and rumors start—fueled by fear, or just plain misunderstanding. Pretty quickly, survivors learn that not everyone knows how to handle the hard truths of violence.
But even with all these challenges, survivors start to reclaim parts of their life. Sometimes, it’s as simple as reaching out to a friend, going back to work, or taking a walk around the block. Every step forward is hard-won, a sign of the resilience that’s quietly building beneath the surface. The trauma doesn’t just vanish, but it can become something to manage—instead of something that defines them.
Survival isn’t a perfect journey. There’ll be setbacks—panic attacks, flashbacks, tough days where despair creeps in. But with time, survivors learn how to navigate this new landscape. Healing is possible, even if it doesn’t look like they imagined. The scars stay, but they stand as reminders of what’s been endured—and overcome.
And through it all, the survivor’s voice gets stronger. At first, they might speak only in whispers. Gradually, confidence grows. Their story becomes a source of strength—not just for themselves, but for anyone else who’s dealing with similar pain. By sharing their truth, survivors reclaim their sense of agency and purpose, turning pain into something that can spark real change.
